Chapter 5. Machine Learning Model Deployment

So far, we’ve explored the individual stages of building and deploying a ML model: data preprocessing, feature engineering, model training, evaluation, and serving. In this chapter, we’ll shift our focus to orchestration and look at how to connect these steps into an automated pipeline that runs reliably in production.

We’ll walk through how to structure end-to-end ML workflows on Databricks, including platform components, workspace design, permission management, and deployment strategies. By the end of the chapter, you’ll understand how to design your ML pipeline using best practices that are suited to the Databricks environment.

Let’s begin with the orchestration of our machine learning pipelines. In Chapter 2, we introduced DABs and examined the structure of the databricks.yml file. What we have not yet looked at are the resources that get deployed when the databricks bundle deploy command runs.

The resources folder is referenced in the bundle definition and includes the following files:

ml_pipeline.yml

This is a Lakeflow job that defines the whole ML pipeline.

ml_monitoring.yml

This is a Lakeflow job that updates the monitoring table.

alert.yml

This file contains alert-related resources.

In this chapter, we focus on the ML pipeline, and in Chapter 6, we’ll turn to monitoring and alerting resources.

Machine Learning Pipeline

Before we examine the structure of the ml_pipeline.yml file, let’s clarify the objective. The file contains a Lakeflow job that brings together data preprocessing, model retraining and evaluation, and model deployment. Figure 5-1 illustrates the pipeline’s architecture, highlighting how it supports retraining and deploying models with built-in conditional logic.

The workflow begins with a preprocessing step that prepares the data. Next, the train_model task retrains the model, evaluates its performance against the latest registered model on the new test set, and registers it if there is an improvement. It sets two task values: model_updated and model_version.

The model_updated task is an IF task in the Lakeflow job. It checks whether a new model was actually registered. If not (i.e., if the task returns model_updated = 0), the job ends early. If a new model was registered (i.e., if the task returns model_updated = 1), the workflow continues to the deploy_model task, which wraps the model as a PyFunc and deploys it to an endpoint using the latest model_version. This setup ensures that only evaluated and improved models are deployed to production.

Each task in the workflow (except the IF task) runs a Python script that requires specific parameters. Some parameters are set by the bundle:

env

This parameter matches the bundle target (e.g., dev, prd).

root_path

This is the root directory of the bundle.

git_sha and branch

These are variables that are defined in the bundle and overwritten by the CI/CD pipeline.

run_id, job_id, and task_name

These are set dynamically, using references like {{job.run_id}} and {{task.name}}, when the job starts.

We need these parameters for a few reasons:

  • They allow the scripts to access the correct configuration files.

  • We can use them to tag experiments, models, and deployments, so we can always trace a result back to the corresponding code and run.

To simplify parameter parsing, we’ll define a create_parser() function in the utils.common module of our package.

First, we define the common arguments among all steps: env and root_path. We then create a common parser that accepts these two arguments, which is used for preprocessing and later for monitoring.

Next, the training and deployment steps require the same arguments, so we create a train_deploy_model parser for them:

def create_parser(args: Sequence[str] = None) -> argparse.Namespace:
   """Create and configure an argument parser for MLOps on Databricks.

   This function sets up a parser with subparsers for different MLOps operations.

   :param args: Optional sequence of command-line argument strings
   :return: Parsed argument namespace
   """
   parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Parser for MLOps on Databricks")
   subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

   # Common arguments
   common_args = argparse.ArgumentParser(add_help=False)
   common_args.add_argument(
       "--root_path", type=str, required=True,
       help="Path of root on DAB")
   common_args.add_argument(
       "--env", type=str, required=True,
       help="Path of env file on DAB")

   # Data ingestion subparser
   subparsers.add_parser("common", parents=[common_args], help="Common processor")

   # Model training & registering subparser
   model_parser = subparsers.add_parser(
       "train_deploy_model",
       parents=[common_args],
       help="Model training and registering")
   model_parser.add_argument(
       "--branch", type=str, required=True,
       help="branch of the project")
   model_parser.add_argument(
       "--git_sha", type=str, required=True,
       help="git sha of the commit")
   model_parser.add_argument(
       "--run_id", type=str, required=True,
       help="run id of the run of the Lakeflow job")
   model_parser.add_argument(
       "--job_id", type=str, required=True,
       help="Lakeflow job id")
   return parser.parse_args(args)

Using this approach means we don’t have to define the argument parsing logic in each script, which simplifies the project code. Let’s now take a deep dive into each of the steps.

Data Preprocessing

Let’s take a look at the ml_pipeline.yml file. It has a resources section where one job, ml-pipeline, is defined. Once deployed, the job will be called hotel-booking-ml-pipeline. It runs based on a schedule (which we can set using Quartz Cron syntax): every Monday at 6:00 a.m. CET. We can set the pause status to PAUSED to nonproduction environments by using the schedule_pause_status bundle variable.

The schedule is illustrative: in practice, to choose the right cadence, you must think carefully about your specific use case. Retraining frequency depends on several factors. You should ask yourself how quickly your data distribution shifts. A recommendation system for a news platform might need daily updates as trending topics change rapidly, while an email classification model for internal processes might remain stable for months. Consider also the cost of retraining versus the cost of degraded performance: if a stale model means lost revenue or poor user experience, more frequent retraining pays for itself.

Triggering retraining only when monitoring detects performance degradation sounds appealing in theory. But in practice, this approach is often impractical. By the time your metrics have degraded enough to trigger retraining, you’re already serving poor predictions to users. Moreover, the degradation itself may signal a deeper problem that retraining won’t fix. If your input data quality has dropped, an upstream system changed its output format, or a key feature has stopped updating, throwing fresh training at the problem won’t help. You’ll just train a new model on the same broken data. But scheduled retraining with robust monitoring catches these issues earlier and keeps the system in a known, predictable state. We’ll talk about monitoring in detail in Chapter 6.

Here is how the schedule for the pipeline is defined in the corresponding resources/ml_pipeline.yml file:

resources:
 jobs:
   ml-pipeline:
     name: hotel-booking-ml-pipeline
     schedule:
       quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 6 ? * MON"
       timezone_id: "Europe/Amsterdam"
       pause_status: "${var.schedule_pause_status}"

We pass a usage policy ID (formerly known as a budget policy ID) for cost monitoring purposes:

budget_policy_id: "${var.usage_policy_id}"

We’ll discuss cost allocation in Chapter 9.

Here, we will use a serverless cluster to run the job. We’ll define an environment called default and select environment version 4, which matches Python 3.12 (which we are using), as we discussed in Chapter 2. Here, we’ll also specify the project dependencies: all .whl files in the dist folder, where the project package built by the bundle is stored. This environment is then referenced in all the tasks:

environments:
  - environment_key: default
    spec:
      environment_version: "4"
      dependencies:
        - ../dist/*.whl

The first task of the job is called preprocessing. It is a spark_python task that runs the preprocess_data.py Python script. Notice that the location of the script is relative to the location of the ml_pipeline.yml file. (It is located in the resources folder.):

tasks:
  - task_key: preprocessing
    environment_key: default
    spark_python_task:
      python_file: ../scripts/preprocess_data.py
      parameters:
        - "common"
        - "--root_path"
        - "${workspace.root_path}"
        - "--env"
        - "${bundle.target}"

You’ll notice that the preprocess_data.py script takes two arguments: env and root_path. The first parameter, common, means that we will use the common parser to parse the arguments. The databricks bundle deploy command uploads all the files that belong to the bundle to a specific location (defined as the root_path). Our data preprocessing code depends on the project_config.yml file, which is stored in the files folder under the root path. Because the root path changes depending on the target, it is convenient to provide it as an argument. In the project_config.yml file, we define the environment-specific values for the catalog and schema. These values match the targets specified in the databricks.yml file, so we can pass the target as an argument.

Inside the preprocess_data.py script, we use the create_parser function we defined earlier to parse the arguments that were passed to the script. We need these arguments to identify the location of the configuration file and load it:

import pandas as pd
import yaml
from loguru import logger
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

from hotel_booking.config import ProjectConfig
from hotel_booking.data.data_processor import DataProcessor
from hotel_booking.utils.common import create_parser

args = create_parser()

cfg = ProjectConfig.from_yaml(
   config_path=f"{args.root_path}/files/project_config.yml", env=args.env
)
logger.info("Configuration loaded:")
logger.info(yaml.dump(cfg, default_flow_style=False))

After that, the code gets really simple. We initialize the DataProcessor class we defined earlier by using the Pandas DataFrame, project configuration, and SparkSession. We preprocess the data, generate 1,000 synthetic observations, and store them in Unity Catalog under the catalog and schema defined in the project_config.yml file:

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

# Load the dataset
df = pd.read_csv(f"{args.root_path}/files/data/booking.csv")

# Initialize DataProcessor
data_processor = DataProcessor(df=df, config=cfg, spark=spark)
data_processor.preprocess()
if spark.catalog.tableExists(data_processor.target_table):
   data_processor.generate_synthetic_df(n=1000, max_date=None)

data_processor.save_to_catalog()

And with that, we’re done with the data preprocessing step! Now, let’s move to the next part: model training.

Training, Evaluating, and Registering a Model

In the databricks.yml file, we’ve defined the branch and git_sha variables, which are passed as parameters in the train_model task, along with other parameters. Here, we’ll use the train_deploy_model parser we defined earlier:

- task_key: "train_model"
  environment_key: default
  depends_on:
    - task_key: "preprocessing"
  spark_python_task:
    python_file: "../scripts/train_register_model.py"
    parameters:
      - "train_deploy_model"
      - "--root_path"
      - "${workspace.root_path}"
      - "--env"
      - "${bundle.target}"
      - "--branch"
      - "${var.branch}"
      - "--git_sha"
      - "${var.git_sha}"
      - "--run_id"
      - "{{job.run_id}}"
      - "--job_id"
      - "{{job.id}}"

This task runs the train_register_model.py Python script. Here, we are mostly going through the same steps as in the “MLflow Evaluation” section of Chapter 3. Just as in the data preprocessing step, we load the project configuration, initialize the SparkSession, and parse the arguments, and then, we use the DataLoader class to load and split the data into the train and the test set:

import mlflow
import yaml
from loguru import logger
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

from hotel_booking.config import ProjectConfig, Tags
from hotel_booking.data.data_loader import DataLoader
from hotel_booking.models.lightgbm_model import LightGBMModel
from hotel_booking.utils.common import create_parser

args = create_parser()

cfg = ProjectConfig.from_yaml(
   config_path=f"{args.root_path}/files/project_config.yml", env=args.env)

logger.info("Configuration loaded:")
logger.info(yaml.dump(cfg, default_flow_style=False))

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

data_loader = DataLoader(spark=spark, config=cfg)
X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = data_loader.split()

After we load the data, we train and log the model. The model metrics dictionary is stored as metrics_new. Notice that we pass actual values of the run_id, git_sha, and branch as tags:

model = LightGBMModel(config=cfg)
tags = Tags(**{"git_sha": args.git_sha, "branch": args.branch, "run_id": args.run_id})
model.train(X_train=X_train, y_train=y_train)
model_info = model.log_model(
   experiment_name="/Shared/hotel-booking-training",
   tags=tags,
   X_test=X_test,
   y_test=y_test,
   train_set_spark=data_loader.train_set_spark,
   train_query=data_loader.train_query,
   test_set_spark=data_loader.test_set_spark,
   test_query=data_loader.test_query,
)

metrics_new = model.metrics

Now, we’ll evaluate the latest registered model (if it exists) on the new test set. If no older registered model with the latest-model alias exists, or if the newly trained model improves on the metric (here, we use root mean squared error as an example), we register it and set the model_updated and model_version task values, which we will use in the follow-up tasks:

sklearn_model_name = f"{cfg.catalog}.{cfg.schema}.hotel_booking_basic"
eval_data = X_test.copy()
eval_data[cfg.target] = y_test

should_register = True
try:
   mlflow.MlflowClient().get_model_version_by_alias(sklearn_model_name, "latest-model")
   model_exists = True
except mlflow.exceptions.RestException:
   model_exists = False
   logger.info(f"No {sklearn_model_name}@latest-model yet. Registering new model.")

if model_exists:
   result = mlflow.models.evaluate(
       model=f"models:/{sklearn_model_name}@latest-model",
       data=eval_data,
       targets=cfg.target,
       model_type="regressor",
       evaluators=["default"],
   )
   rmse_old = result.metrics["root_mean_squared_error"]
   rmse_new = metrics_new["root_mean_squared_error"]
   should_register = rmse_new < rmse_old
   logger.info(
       f"Current RMSE {rmse_old:.4f}, new RMSE {rmse_new:.4f} -> "
       + ("registering new model" if should_register else "keeping current model")
   )

if should_register:
   model_version = model.register_model(model_name=sklearn_model_name, tags=tags)
   dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="model_version", value=model_version)
   dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="model_updated", value=1)
else:
   dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="model_updated", value=0)

Deploying a Model Serving Endpoint

The model_updated task defines whether the pipeline will run further. It checks whether the model_updated task value is equal to 1: if the condition evaluates to true, the job proceeds to the final step, deploy_model task. It takes the same arguments as the train_model task:

- task_key: model_updated
  condition_task:
    op: "EQUAL_TO"
    left: "{{tasks.train_model.values.model_updated}}"
    right: "1"
  depends_on:
    - task_key: "train_model"

- task_key: "deploy_model"
  environment_key: default
  depends_on:
    - task_key: "model_updated"
      outcome: "true"
  spark_python_task:
    python_file: "../scripts/deploy_model.py"
    parameters:
      - "train_deploy_model"
      - "--root_path"
      - "${workspace.root_path}"
      - "--env"
      - "${bundle.target}"
      - "--branch"
      - "${var.branch}"
      - "--git_sha"
      - "${var.git_sha}"
      - "--run_id"
      - "{{job.run_id}}"
      - "--job_id"
      - "{{job.id}}"

The task runs the deploy_model.py script. After loading the project configuration and parsing the arguments, we retrieve the model_version task value from the train_model task. We then use it to look up the corresponding ModelInfo instance:

import mlflow
from loguru import logger

from hotel_booking.config import ProjectConfig, Tags
from hotel_booking.models.pyfunc_model_wrapper import HotelBookingModelWrapper
from hotel_booking.models.serving import serve_model
from hotel_booking.utils.common import create_parser

args = create_parser()

model_version = dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(
   taskKey="train_model",
   key="model_version")
logger.info(f"Retrieved wrapped model version: {model_version}")

cfg = ProjectConfig.from_yaml(
   config_path=f"{args.root_path}/files/project_config.yml", env=args.env)

model_name = f"{cfg.catalog}.{cfg.schema}.hotel_booking_pyfunc"
wrapped_model_name = f"{cfg.catalog}.{cfg.schema}.hotel_booking_basic"

wrapped_model_info = mlflow.models.get_model_info(
    model_uri=f"models:/{wrapped_model_name}/{model_version}"
)

We then use that to log and register the wrapper with its dependencies:

wrapper = HotelBookingModelWrapper()

with open(f"{args.root_path}/files/version.txt") as f:
   version = f.read().strip()
whl_name = f"hotel_booking-{version}-py3-none-any.whl"
code_paths = [f"{args.root_path}/artifacts/.internal/{whl_name}"]

tags = Tags(**{"git_sha": args.git_sha,
              "branch": args.branch,
              "run_id": args.run_id})

model_version = wrapper.log_register_model(
   wrapped_model_info=wrapped_model_info,
   pyfunc_model_name=model_name,
   experiment_name="/Shared/hotel-booking-pyfunc",
   code_paths=code_paths,
   tags=tags,
)

After we have registered the model, we can finally deploy it using the serve_model function that we defined earlier (and that you can find in the models.serving module) and finish our pipeline:

serve_model(
   entity_name=model_name,
   entity_version=model_version,
   budget_policy_id=cfg.usage_policy_id,
   endpoint_name="hotel-booking-pyfunc",
   schema_name=cfg.schema,
   catalog_name=cfg.catalog,
   table_name_prefix="hotel_booking_monitoring",
)

As mentioned earlier, we should view PyFunc more as a FastAPI model wrapper and should keep it separate from the model training logic. That way, we won’t necessarily have to retrain it if the payload logic needs to change.

So far, we’ve been using serverless compute to run our jobs. Now, let’s look at another Lakeflow job that explicitly defines a classic cluster configuration instead. In this example, we use classic compute purely for demonstration purposes, to show how cluster specifications work within a job definition. However, if you are working in the Databricks Free Edition, you should update the configuration to use serverless compute, as it is the only option available in that environment.

Serverless versus Classic Compute for Lakeflow Jobs

In the resources folder, you can find another yml file called ml_monitoring.yml, which defines the hotel-booking-monitor-update job.

This job is configured to run daily at 9:00 CET, and its schedule can be paused depending on the bundle deployment target (e.g., development, production). The job cluster, where we can set many different configurations, is defined, and we can use this cluster to run the scripts/refresh_monitor.py Python script:

resources:
 jobs:
   house-price-monitor-update:
     name: hotel-booking-monitor-update-workflow
     schedule:
       quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 9 * * ?"
       timezone_id: "Europe/Amsterdam"
       pause_status: "${var.schedule_pause_status}"
     tags:
       project_name: "hotel-booking"

     job_clusters:
       - job_cluster_key: "hotel-booking-cluster"
         new_cluster:
           spark_version: "17.3.x-scala2.13"
           data_security_mode: "SINGLE_USER"
           node_type_id: "r3.xlarge"
           driver_node_type_id: "r3.xlarge"
           num_workers: 1

     tasks:
       - task_key: "refresh_monitor_table"
         job_cluster_key: "hotel-booking-cluster"
         spark_python_task:
           python_file: "../scripts/refresh_monitor.py"
           parameters:
             - "common"
             - "--root_path"
             - "${workspace.root_path}"
             - "--env"
             - "${bundle.target}"
         libraries:
          - whl: ../dist/*.whl

Notice that we do not provide a usage policy ID in the job definition, as it can only be applied to serverless resources. Instead, we pass a tag for cost allocation.

We can also override the job’s default cluster with an interactive cluster by specifying the cluster_id argument for a given target. For example, it’s common practice to do this in the dev target to speed up iteration and debugging. In this setup, jobs run directly on an existing interactive cluster, rather than spinning up a new one. Additionally, we set the dynamic_version setting for artifacts to true, to ensure that the latest version of the package is always installed whenever the code changes, which is helpful during active development:

targets:
 dev:
  default: true
  mode: development
  cluster_id: 0513-112814-kzixtb9s
  workspace:
    host: <your_host>
    root_path: "/Workspace/Users/${workspace.current_user.userName}/\
              .bundle/${bundle.target}/${bundle.name}"
  artifacts:
    default:
      type: whl
      build: uv build
      path: .
      dynamic_version: true

In Chapter 6, we’ll cover the monitoring job in detail, including its role in tracking model performance. For now, our focus is on how serverless jobs differ from jobs that utilize classic jobs compute, which can be useful if more customization is required.

So far, we’ve worked entirely in a development environment, without worrying about how code and models move across environments. But to address promotion strategies, we’ll first need to understand the basics of Databricks platform design, including workspace structure, environment isolation, and compute options. That foundation is key for managing ML workflows in production.

Databricks Platform Design

We have already interacted with various components of the Databricks platform and experienced the Databricks workspace—a user interface that allows developers to create, access, and manage various Databricks assets, such as experiments, models, and jobs. It is common for organizations to have more than one workspace and use separate workspaces to isolate Databricks assets from other environments, teams, and even data and AI products.

We’ve also interacted with Unity Catalog: we used it to create Delta tables and register models. For a workspace to use Unity Catalog, it must be attached to a Unity Catalog metastore, which is the top-level container for metadata of all data and AI assets. You can have one metastore per cloud region, and you can only attach a workspace to one metastore in the same cloud region. It is not uncommon for large organizations with international operations to have multiple Unity Catalog metastores.

In Unity Catalog, assets are organized using the following a three-tier hierarchy within the metastore:

  1. Catalogs, which are the highest level of organization.

  2. Schemas, which are contained within catalogs.

  3. Assets, which include the tables, views, volumes, models, and functions within schemas. We refer to these assets with this three-part naming convention: catalog.schema.asset.

Figure 5-2 depicts this hierarchy.

All the workspaces belong to a Databricks account. Databricks account admin permissions are needed to create and manage workspaces and Unity Catalog metastores, and they’re also needed to configure settings on the account level (such as by enabling certain features). Figure 5-3 depicts the relationships among accounts, metastores and workspaces.

I’ve mentioned that you may want to have different Databricks workspaces for different environments, but how many environments do you actually need? Let’s look at that next.

How Many Environments Do You Need?

The development, testing, acceptance, and production (DTAP) approach is probably the most common one in the industry.

One of the earliest formalizations of DTAP came from Cal Evans in 2009.1 He noted that “The structure of development environments hasn’t radically changed over the past 20 years.” That means the DTAP pattern is now over 35 years old, so it predates cloud computing, IaC, and the widespread adoption of version control.

Consider what the software development sequence looked like before DTAP emerged:

  1. Development happened first, on individual laptops or desktops. Developers had access to a shared development server and database, which was often populated with a stale copy of production data. They’d manually copy files to the server via FTP or basic scripts. Version control existed via the Concurrent Versions System (CVS) or Subversion, but it wasn’t universal. Git was only invented in 2005.

  2. Testing came next and was where code got integrated. On a predetermined schedule, the testing server would check out all the code, refresh the database, and execute testing scripts. Unit tests ran first, and integration and regression tests ran next to verify that all the pieces fit together and nothing that was previously working had gotten broken. (We’ll talk about testing at the end of this chapter.) Quality assurance (QA) engineers owned this environment, but they had no access to production data.

  3. Acceptance came after testing, and mirrored production in services and revision levels. This was where developers lost control: operations and release engineers took over. When code was ready for release, it was checked out onto the Acceptance server. Teams often re-ran integration and regression tests as a final sanity check. This was where the client actually saw and tested the code, using their own test plan.

  4. Production deployment was the final phase. At the time, Cal optimistically wrote, “If all goes well, this should be a fully automated process—or, at least, a highly automated operation.” In practice, it was anything but. Deployments happened in scheduled maintenance windows, often on weekends, with extensive sign-offs and manual steps.

The DTAP gates weren’t just about catching bugs; they encoded organizational boundaries. Developers owned development and testing. Operations owned acceptance and production. Code was thrown “over the wall” between these silos.

This made sense in a world where the following things were true:

  • Environments were expensive physical servers, which were impossible to reproduce reliably.

  • Deployments were manual, risky, and infrequent.

  • A bad deployment could mean hours or days of downtime, and rollbacks were slow.

  • CI/CD tooling barely existed. (Jenkins, then called Hudson, appeared in 2005 but wasn’t mainstream.)

DTAP was a safety net for a world without better options. The organizational separation between dev and ops was a feature, not a bug: it forced deliberate handoffs and human verification at each stage.

But by the late 2000s, DevOps culture began challenging this model. If one team owned the entire cycle from development to production, did it really need four separate environments with formal handoffs among them?

Today, especially for ML/AI development, having three environments (development, acceptance, and production) is enough, for the following reasons:

  • ML/AI development comes with certain requirements, such as access to production data in the development environment. This means we achieve a higher level of confidence that the system performs as expected at an earlier stage.

  • IaC makes environments reproducible. We can deploy to development, acceptance, and production environments with identical configurations and security guidelines. This solves environment drift, which is one of DTAP’s core problems.

  • CI/CD is mature. Automated pipelines can build, test, and deploy code in minutes. The manual handoffs that DTAP formalized are now bottlenecks, not safeguards.

  • Teams that follow DevOps principles and own code from development through production don’t need organizational gates between environments.

However, you need to be aware that having four environments may still be necessary in regulated industries, such as critical infrastructure, finance, and health care, where multi-environment gates ensure safety for the users and serve as proof of compliance.

The Big Book of MLOps,2 which was developed by Databricks, also mentions three environments: dev, acc, and prd. We use the three-environment setup in this book as well.

Platform Best Practices

Let’s discuss an example of a Databricks platform setup. It’s common for each individual product, a business unit, or a team to have a set of Databricks workspaces, one per environment—dev, acc, and prd—and a schema or a set of schemas in environment-specific catalogs (mlops_dev, mlops_acc, and mlops_prd). Figure 5-4 illustrates this structure.

ML teams act as both data consumers and data producers: they use curated datasets created by data engineering teams for training the models, and they generate outputs like predictions or embeddings that are consumed by downstream systems. The data that ML teams consume is stored in catalogs related to data products, while the data they produce is stored under ML product schemas in MLOps catalogs.

Data engineering teams commonly organize source data by using the medallion architecture, with separate catalogs for each environment and layer: <env>_bronze, <env>_silver, and <env>_gold:

Bronze

This layer holds raw, ingested data.

Silver

This layer includes cleaned and structured tables.

Gold

This layer contains business-ready datasets.

Each data source or product has a dedicated schema, which enables clear ownership and structured access control.

An important best practice is for the platform team to be able to read production data during development while strictly controlling where they can write data. In practice, ML teams should be able to read data product schemas from the production Gold catalog (prd_gold), even when working from the development workspace. This ensures that training and inference use the same data definitions and quality guarantees across all environments.

Lower-environment copies of data often differ in subtle but important ways (e.g., missing history, relaxed quality checks, schema drift). This can lead to issues that only appear in production, but using production Gold data for development significantly reduces these risks and helps minimize model drift.

At the same time, write access must remain environment specific. From each ML workspace (dev, acc, and prd), teams can write data only to their own schemas in an environment-specific ML catalog (mlops_dev, mlops_acc, or mlops_prd). This prevents accidental pollution of production assets, keeps environment promotion explicit, and maintains clear ownership boundaries.

For platform teams, this pattern balances consistency and safety. Data product teams retain ownership of Gold datasets in prd_gold, while ML teams consume them as read-only dependencies. All ML-generated artifacts are isolated in ML-owned catalogs. With Unity Catalog governance and read-only permissions, exposing production data for development is low risk and avoids the operational burden of maintaining multiple “production-like” data copies.

This structure enables modular, secure development across teams. Data engineers focus on building trusted data products, while ML teams build and deploy models independently on a consistent foundation of production-grade data.

I’ve just mentioned a number of things related to permissions, and that raises another important point: when you’re designing a Databricks platform, you need to have an access control strategy.

Access Control Strategy

In Databricks, access controls are applied at two distinct levels: the workspace level and the Unity Catalog level. Access is governed through securables—objects that can have permissions assigned to them. See Figure 5-5 for a list of securables.

Workspace securables include items like notebooks, dashboards, endpoints, clusters, and jobs, and access to them is managed within each individual workspace. Unity Catalog securables include catalogs, schemas, tables, and other data or AI assets, and access to them is defined at the metastore level.

Workspace securables are managed through access control lists (ACLs).3 Workspace admins have the CAN_MANAGE permission on all objects in their workspace (including clusters), while users have the CAN_MANAGE permission on objects they create.

Unity Catalog securables are managed through privileges.4 Metastore admins can create catalogs, manage permissions, and transfer ownership for any object, read and update the metadata of all objects in the metastore, and even delete a metastore. While metastore admins don’t have direct read or write access to data by default, they can grant themselves access by transferring ownership.

Consider a ML engineer working on two projects simultaneously: hotel booking pricing and demand forecasting. Each project has its own set of Databricks workspaces and Unity Catalogs. To prevent the engineer from accessing demand forecasting data while working in the hotel booking pricing workspace, you can use workspace binding.

Unity Catalog supports two access modes for securables: OPEN and ISOLATED. In OPEN mode, the securable can be accessed from any workspace. In ISOLATED mode, access is restricted to a specified list of workspaces.

Let’s review how we can organize the permissions for a team working on the hotel booking pricing project. Figure 5-6 outlines the permissions for the team and service principals on the workspace level.

The team should have permanent access to the development Databricks workspace, where most experimentation, model development, and collaboration happen. Workspace admin access should be limited to senior engineers or tech leads. Granting admin rights to all users is risky, as it enables unrestricted cluster creation and other unnecessary permissions. A better approach is to create a Databricks group and assign cluster policies that limit what kind of clusters that group can create. It is also important to keep in mind that this setup introduces collaboration challenges in development environments. The user who creates an object—such as a notebook, query, job, or Model Serving endpoint—must explicitly grant the appropriate permissions to the group so that other users can view, edit, or run shared assets.

Access to the acceptance (acc) and production (prd) workspaces should be restricted by default and only granted temporarily when needed, such as for testing deployment pipelines or investigating production issues. This temporary elevated access minimizes risks while still supporting operational needs.

Additionally, service principals (SPNs) are used for automation and CI/CD pipelines. Each environment has a dedicated SPN with scoped permissions that are limited to its corresponding workspace. This separation ensures that automation processes only operate within their intended boundaries and follow the principle of least privilege.

Figure 5-7 shows the permissions for the team and service principals on the Unity Catalog level.

The hotel booking team has ALL_PRIVILEGES permissions on the mlops_dev.hotel_booking schema. In other environments (mlops_acc, mlops_prd, and prd_gold), they have read-only access (SELECT, READ_VOLUME, and EXECUTE), which allows them safe use of production data for training and validation.

SPNs have ALL_PRIVILEGES access on schemas in the corresponding catalogs (mlops_dev, mlops_acc, and mlops_prd) and read-only access to prd_gold.hotel_booking to ensure consistent data consumption across environments, without risk of modifying production data. The privileges on the schema level are propagated to all underlying objects.

Promoting Code and Models to Higher Environments

Now that we’ve covered how different environments (dev, acc, and prd) are structured and secured, we can look at how code and models move among them. First, let’s talk about code promotion, which is tightly coupled with Git branching strategy. Let’s explore how Git serves as the backbone of deployment in a multi-environment Databricks setup.

Git Branching Model

Anyone who uses version control has probably come across Gitflow, which is a branching model created by Vincent Driessen. After Driessen published the post titled “A Successful Git Branching Model” in 2010,5 Gitflow became the default branching strategy for many teams over the following years.

This model assumes two default branches, development and main, along with multiple long-lived feature and release branches. This structure often leads to unnecessary complexity and a lot of branches to manage (see Figure 5-8).

As Vincent mentions in his note of reflection for his original blog,6 dated 2020, the world of software has changed since 2010, and for most teams, it is no longer necessary to support multiple versions of software. For modern applications that require continuous delivery, he recommends a simpler approach called GitHub flow, which is a Git branching model developed and used by GitHub. In this model, developers work on short-lived feature branches and create pull requests to the main branch. This development has become popular over the past few years because of its simplicity.

In the past, I’ve tried to adapt Gitflow to ML projects, and I’ve found it overly complicated. All the ML projects I work on follow the GitHub flow development model, which is easier to understand and does not create unnecessary overhead for ML teams.

Here’s how the GitHub flow approach works:

  1. A feature branch feature/foo is created from the main branch. After a number of commits, the branch is ready.

  2. A developer creates a pull request (PR).

  3. At PR to the main branch, a CI pipeline run gets triggered.

  4. It runs pre-commit checks and unit tests. An approval is required to merge the pull request.

  5. When the feature branch is merged to main, a CD pipeline run gets triggered and targets two environments: acceptance and production.

  6. The CD pipeline in the acceptance environment can run directly, but deployment to the production environment should be approved by a reviewer first. Usually, some manual checks on the acceptance environment are required to make sure everything works as expected.

  7. Figure 5-9 provides a simplified illustration of this GitHub flow approach.

Let’s now take a close look at the CI and CD pipelines, which I mentioned previously when explaining the Git branching strategy.

Continuous Integration Pipeline

Let’s take a look at the continuous integration (CI) pipeline for the MLOps part of the book (from the ci_mlops.yml file in the .github/workflows folder), which is triggered to run on each PR to the main branch if files in the mlops folder have changed:

on:
 pull_request:
   branches:
     - 'main'
   paths:
     - 'mlops/**'

The pipeline has one job. The first step in this job is to check out the repository under GitHub workspace, so the workflow can access the code. Notice that we fetch the history of all branches and tags by setting fetch_depth to 0 (the default is 1), to make sure that the next step can run correctly:

jobs:
 pytest_and_checks:
   runs-on: ubuntu-latest
   steps:
     - uses: actions/checkout@de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd #v6.0.2
       with:
         # Fetch all history for all branches and tags
         fetch-depth: 0
         ref: ${{ github.head_ref }}

The following steps install uv and all the dependencies, and they run pre-commit checks and PyTest:

- name: Install uv
  uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@0cec208311dfd045dd5311c1add060b2062131d57 #v8.0.0

- name: Install the dependencies
  run: |
    uv sync --extra ci

- name: Run pre-commit checks
  run: |
    uv run pre-commit run --all-files

- name: run pytest
  run: |
    uv run pytest

It’s also important to note that we do not use tags but instead commit hash for public GitHub Actions. This is a good security practice that minimizes the risk of malicious attacks, which can happen if the tag gets overwritten by a malicious actor.7

Continuous Deployment Pipeline

Let’s take a look at the continuous deployment (CD) pipeline, which is triggered to run on push to the main branch if files in the mlops folder have changed:

on:
 push:
   branches:
     - 'main'
   paths:
     - 'mlops/**'

This pipeline defines a single deployment job with a matrix strategy, which allows the same job definition to run across multiple environments using variable combinations. In this case, the job runs twice (once each in the acc and prd environments), based on the values defined in the matrix.

GitHub environments are used to manage environment-specific variables, secrets, and federated credentials under a consistent name. By referencing ${{ matrix.environment }}, the job dynamically applies the appropriate configuration for each run.

The job requires specific permissions:

id-token

This is write permission to fetch an OpenID Connect (OIDC) token for authentication.

contents

This is write permission to push a Git tag after a successful production deployment.

The DATABRICKS_HOST environment variable is set using the GitHub environment-specific variable with the same name:

jobs:
 deploy:
   runs-on: ubuntu-latest
   strategy:
     matrix:
       environment: [acc, prd]
   environment: ${{ matrix.environment }}
   permissions:
     id-token: write # to fetch openID token
     contents: write # to push tag
   env:
     DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ vars.DATABRICKS_HOST }}

The first step checks out the repository under GitHub workspace:

steps:
  - name: Checkout Source Code
    uses: actions/checkout@de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd #v6.0.2

In this example, we use Amazon Web Services (AWS), so we configure AWS authentication and retrieve Databricks credentials from AWS Secrets Manager. We could have used a similar process for Azure or Google Cloud Platform (GCP). This setup enables secure access to Databricks during deployment. Note that in such a case, our cluster specification would need modification as well.

The second step uses the configure-aws-credentials GitHub action to assume an identity and access management (IAM) role defined in the ARN_ROLE variable and then set the AWS region. This grants the pipeline temporary credentials to access AWS resources.

The third step fetches secrets from AWS Secrets Manager by using those credentials. The secret contains two key-value pairs: DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET. These values are exported as environment variables with the same names, which are then used to authenticate with Databricks when running databricks bundle deploy. Note that the Databricks CLI requires three environment variables for authentication with the service principal: DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID, DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET, and DATABRICKS_HOST:

- name: Configure AWS credentials
  uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials
        @ec61189d14ec14c8efccab744f656cffd0e33f37 #v6.1.0
  with:
    role-to-assume: ${{ vars.ARN_ROLE }}
    aws-region: eu-west-1

- name: Fetch secrets
  uses: aws-actions/aws-secretsmanager-get-secrets
        @2cb1a461cbd4865ac4299648312e4704c646cd53 #v3.0.1
  with:
    secret-ids: |
      , ${{ vars.SECRET_ID }}
    parse-json-secrets: true

The final steps in the pipeline prepare the deployment environment and handle promotion logic for production. First, the Databricks CLI is installed using the official setup action. This is required to run the databricks bundle deploy command, which publishes the bundle definition to the target environment.

Next, the uv package manager is installed. It’s used to build any Python packages defined in the bundle configuration. Finally, the deployment step runs databricks bundle deploy, passing the current git sha as a variable. Note that deploying a bundle does not trigger any jobs. Instead, jobs will run based on defined triggers within the Databricks workflow:

- name: Install Databricks CLI
  uses: databricks/setup-cli@2260866f83a41a2df55e1cfe7ffe038b78325bf6 #v0.295.0
  with:
    version: 0.295.0

- name: Install uv
  uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@0cec208311dfd045dd5311c1add060b2062131d57 #v8.0.0

- name: Deploy to Databricks
  env:
    DATABRICKS_BUNDLE_ENV: ${{ matrix.environment }}
  run: databricks bundle deploy --var="git_sha=${{ github.sha }}"

In our CD pipeline example, we have authenticated with AWS using federated credentials that are set up for each GitHub environment. However, before we can do that in the real world, we need to create a set of service principals on Databricks and a set of IAM roles, policies, and secrets on AWS.

OpenID Connect

Figure 5-10 shows an example of the setup. It assumes that we have three different Databricks workspaces (dev, acc, and prd). Each of these workspaces contains a service principal, and the client secret and client id of these service principals are stored in the respective secrets in AWS Secret Manager. We also need to create custom IAM policies that allow us to read these secrets from the secret manager. These policies are attached to the respective IAM roles, which are assumed when CI/CD pipelines get executed under their respective environments.

You can find the trust policy definition for the IAM role. Please note that you must create an OpenID Connect identity provider by setting provider to token.actions.githubusercontent.com and audience to sts.amazonaws.com:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated":
    "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
        },
        "StringLike": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub":
            "repo:ORG_NAME/REPO_NAME:environment:ENVIRONMENT_NAME"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

In our setup, we do not use GitHub secrets. Instead, we use the OIDC setup, which is generally considered to be a more secure solution. However, we use environment variables that contain different values in each environment. Figure 5-11 shows the view of configured environments in GitHub.

Here are example values for the variables in the development environment:

  • ARN_ROLE: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/GitHubDevOIDC

  • DATABRICKS_HOST: https://dbc-c2e8445d-159d.cloud.databricks.com

  • SECRET_ID: dev_dbr

Using CI/CD pipelines alone is not sufficient to ensure secure deployments. When I described the GitHub flow, I mentioned the approval step multiple times. We can configure this step by using the branch and deployment protection rules to enforce a manual review before code is merged or deployed. Let’s dive into it.

Branch and deployment protection rules

Implementing branch protection rules is essential for preventing developers from committing directly to important branches, like main. GitHub offers rich functionality for these rules, but some of them are more critical than others. While features like requiring status checks to pass are nice to have, I believe the absolute minimum for any project is to enable the “Require a pull request before merging” rule, along with the sub-options shown in Figure 5-12.

These include the following:

  • Requiring at least one (ideally, two) approvals

  • Requiring a review if a new commit is pushed after the pull request is approved

  • Using the CODEOWNERS file: automatically assigning reviewers based on the code being changed

  • Enforcing approval: requiring the most recent push to be approved by someone other than the person who pushed it

I also recommend enabling the “Do not bypass the above settings” option to ensure these rules cannot be circumvented.

I mentioned earlier that deployment to production should be approved by a reviewer. We can enable this by using the deployment protection rules that are selected in Figure 5-13, which we can set for each environment and repository. These rules provide necessary guardrails without making the CD pipelines more complicated than they need to be.

So far, we’ve explored key considerations for promoting code across environments to ensure secure and reliable deployment. We assumed two things: models are retrained independently in each environment, and retraining is stateless, starting from scratch every time. But this isn’t always realistic.

For deep learning models, which can be large and expensive to train, it’s often preferable to resume training from previously saved weights. In these cases, you typically want to train the model once, often in a development environment, and promote it without retraining. However, copying models between Unity Catalogs (e.g., from dev to acc to prd) is not the best approach. Instead, it is more efficient to use a shared Unity Catalog, where the model is stored once and promotion is handled through aliases and approval workflows, rather than physical duplication. Let’s discuss how you can accomplish this.

Promoting Models to Higher Environments

Let’s say the ML team is working on updating the weights for the hotel booking embedding model in the Databricks development workspace. The resulting model is registered in the central Unity Catalog, and it should eventually be deployed behind a Model Serving endpoint in the Databricks production workspace. Figure 5-14 demonstrates how to do this in a secure way.

In this workflow, the embedding model is managed centrally in the mlops_shared.hotel_booking.embeddings catalog and promoted across environments using MLflow aliases. The model is large, so it cannot be trained locally. After updating weights in the development workspace, the model is registered and assigned the latest-dev alias.

In the simplest scenario, the model update did not require the code change, but we still need to store references to the updated model version in the configuration file (for example, project_config.yml). A PR to the main branch gets created, and it triggers tests and requires code review. After the code is merged to the main branch, the CD pipeline gets triggered, and deployment to acceptance and production gets executed there. Deployment to production is protected and requires approval. Earlier in the chapter, we looked at the CD pipeline, which only updates the Lakeflow job definition, but it can also trigger the execution of the Lakeflow job.

In the acceptance environment, the Lakeflow job gets the model version by latest-dev alias, verifies that the model version matches the one defined in the configuration file, and evaluates the model. For embeddings, programmatic evaluation typically involves computing similarity scores or ranking quality using predefined benchmarks or labeled pairs. If the evaluation confirms that the model performs as expected, the alias is updated to latest-acc and the model is deployed to the acceptance endpoint. A similar process follows in the production workspace, where we get the model version by latest-acc alias, assuming that the pipeline ran in the acceptance environment first.

In the approach we’ve discussed, the model stays in a shared catalog, and promotion across environments is handled through aliases and code promotion. This is gated by a manual approval step, rather than by duplicating the model. This setup enables efficient, auditable, and environment-aware model lifecycle management.

Earlier, when we built the CI pipeline, testing showed up as a single step. It is easy to treat this as a checkbox and move on, but it deserves a closer look. What actually belongs in that step, and why ML systems ask more of it than ordinary software does, is the subject of the next section.

Testing

Many ML practitioners have converged on the same observation: production incidents frequently originate from data quality issues, schema changes, feature pipeline failures, training-serving skew, deployment mistakes, and monitoring gaps, rather than flaws in the underlying model architecture.

Jeremy Jordan, a core maintainer of PyTorch Lightning, explains what goes into effective testing in his blog.8 Developing ML models relies on a large amount of traditional software development: processing data, building features, orchestrating training, and exposing interfaces to external systems. Effective testing of ML systems therefore requires both a traditional software testing suite for the surrounding infrastructure and a model testing suite for the trained artifacts.

In this section of the book, we limit ourselves to practical considerations, since testing could be a whole book on its own. You can find test examples in the repository that accompanies this book.

ML Model Testing

Model tests are divided into pre-train tests and post-train tests:

Pre-train tests

These run before training and short-circuit a wasted job: the output shape matches the labels, class probabilities sum to one, a single gradient step decreases the loss, and there is no label leakage between the training and validation sets.

Post-train tests

These interrogate the behavior the model actually learned. They include the following kinds of tests:

Invariance tests

These are tests for perturbations that must not change the prediction.

Directional expectation tests

These are tests for perturbations that must change the prediction in a known direction (e.g., more bathrooms should not lower a predicted house price).

Minimum functionality tests

These are tests on critical data slices.

It is also important not to confuse model evaluation with model testing:

Model evaluation

This summarizes performance and tells you whether the model is good on average. We performed model evaluation earlier in this book, before registering a model for deployment.

Model testing

This consists of explicit checks for specific behaviors the model must exhibit.

The distinction between these two matters, because an evaluation can improve overall while introducing a regression or bias on an important slice of data.

There are also tests for data specifically: assertions about datasets, schemas, null and range constraints, and distribution expectations. On Databricks, DQX provides declarative checks of this kind, and the same idea extends to monitoring the input tables that feed your processing pipelines.

We won’t go deep into any of these here. They sit on top of a more fundamental layer. The rest of this section focuses on software engineering tests and their Databricks-specific considerations, because that foundation is where ML teams most often underinvest. For concrete model testing examples, read Eugene Yan’s blog.9

Software Testing

For decades, software engineering has organized tests around the test pyramid: there are many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and a small number of end-to-end tests at the top. Figure 5-15 shows the test pyramid on Databricks that follows the same idea. We’ll explain the details later.

The trade-off is simple: as tests become more realistic, they also become slower, more expensive, and harder to debug. The goal is to catch everything you can at the cheapest layer and reserve higher-level tests for what only they can verify. The same model applies to ML systems on Databricks.

There is a lot of great literature on software testing. These are the ones we particularly recommend:

  • Effective Testing: From Slop to Software by Matt Harrison (self-pub.)

  • Python Testing with pytest by Brian Okken (O’Reilly)

Let’s go through the layers one by one, but not in too much detail, as whole books are devoted to this topic.

Unit testing

A unit test isolates a small piece of logic and runs entirely locally: with no Databricks workspace, no cluster startup, no Unity Catalog access, and no network calls. These are the cheapest tests you have: they run in milliseconds, give deterministic feedback, and execute on every commit. They catch obvious mistakes early, and with AI-assisted development tools, writing them is practically free. There is no longer any excuse to skip them.

Your code does use actual SDK clients, and since we do not want to use them, we need to mock. Python’s unittest.mock and pytest-mock make this straightforward.

You should mock only at genuine system boundaries such as REST APIs, SDK clients, and storage systems, and you should use real objects for code within your application. Excessive mocking couples tests with implementation details and produces suites that stay green while the system is broken.

Two rules prevent most mistakes:

  • Patch where the name is looked up, not where it is defined. Patch the import used by the module under test, not the module that defines the object.

  • Use autospec=True whenever possible. A mock with autospec derives its interface from the real object, so if a method is renamed, removed, or given different parameters, the test fails immediately. Without it, mocks accept attributes and signatures that no longer exist, so they produce green tests over broken code.

Databricks considerations

For Databricks projects, we reserve unit tests for logic that’s expressible independently of the platform: data transformations on plain Python values, configuration parsing, prompt construction, request validation, and business rules. If a test needs a running cluster, a workspace, or a catalog, it belongs in the integration layer.

Spark transformations are where unit testing on Databricks becomes complicated. Ideally, we would test them against a local Spark session that’s running entirely in memory. In a standard PySpark project, this is straightforward: we install pyspark, create a local SparkSession, and run transformations against small test DataFrames.

The complication is that databricks-connect and pyspark are mutually exclusive. Once databricks-connect is installed, local Spark sessions become unavailable. Also, databricks-connect is pulled in by the version of databricks-agents we use in the book.10

One way out is to keep these dependencies out of the project’s core library and install them only in the job environment that executes the workload. We can then test the transformation code locally with pyspark. This works, but it requires discipline and makes the dependency setup more error-prone. We take the simpler route: we accept that all Spark execution goes through databricks-connect, which brings us to integration testing.

Integration testing

There are two levels of integration testing on Databricks:

  • The first level runs Spark logic on Databricks compute. Once Spark execution goes through databricks-connect, tests that exercise Spark logic run remotely rather than locally. The spark fixture from databricks-labs-pytester is exactly this: a Databricks Connect–backed session, rather than a local one. It still isolates a single transformation, uses small datasets, and gives fast feedback, but its execution is remote. These tests run against remote Spark on serverless compute, execute quickly, and can be launched directly from an IDE. They occupy the role that local Spark unit tests play in a standard PySpark project.

  • The second level validates an entire pipeline end to end: workflow orchestration, task dependencies, parameter flow, permissions, and persistence to Unity Catalog. A typical pattern is to create temporary schemas, trigger the deployed job, assert on the resulting tables, and clean up afterward.

  • At this level, the job definition itself is part of the system under test. Many failures originate not in the code but in the configuration: there may be a missing wheel, an incorrect environment_key, a broken task dependency, or a parameter wired to the wrong task. When pipelines are defined through DABs, these failures are easy to test. The databricks bundle validate test catches definition errors before execution starts, and deployment to an isolated target is itself a test. A failed deployment is a failed test.

Taras Chaikovsk describes integration testing patterns on Databricks in detail in the Databricks community technical blog.11

Practical considerations: Integration tests in CI

The orchestrated ML pipeline can run as part of CI, on a small data sample, to confirm that the whole thing is wired together. A run that samples data, assembles features, and then trains, evaluates, registers, and deploys a model exercises every wiring decision in a way no isolated test can.

The obstacle is duration. Even on sampled data, a run takes long enough that you do not want a GitHub runner to wait until the job finishes. The pattern that avoids this is asynchronous (see Figure 5-16).

The CI workflow validates the bundle, deploys it to the test target, triggers the job run, sets the commit status to pending through the GitHub Commit Status API, and exits green. The commit SHA is passed in as a job parameter so the run can report back against the right commit.

A commit status can be error, failure, pending, or success, and it will surface on any PR involving the commit. A commit status can include target_url and description: the URL points to the Databricks run output, the description summarizes what happened, and both make the status useful in the GitHub UI. The context field names the service that is reporting the status (for example databricks/pipeline-integration), so this check stays distinct from other checks on the same commit. The repo:status OAuth scope grants access to statuses without granting access to repository code.

The run reports its own results through two tasks at the end of the job. One runs with run_if: ALL_SUCCESS and posts success. The other runs with run_if: AT_LEAST_ONE_FAILED and posts failure. Splitting it in two is what makes failure reportable: a single final task runs only on full success, so a failure anywhere would leave the commit stuck on pending. Each task knows its outcome from the condition that triggered it, so neither has to inspect the run. Both reporters depend on every pipeline task, not just the last one, so any task that fails is a direct dependency failure the condition can see. The full lifecycle is three writes: pending at trigger time and then exactly one of success or failure.

Branch protection turns that status into a merge gate. You should mark the status context as a required status check. The pull request stays pending until a reporter fires, and merging is blocked until the check is green.

Notice that Figure 5-16 also lists data tests, model tests, and endpoint payload tests that confirm the output is what we expect. These can run as part of the Lakeflow job. The first level of integration testing, which consists of the Spark tests on Databricks compute, runs in the CI pipeline alongside the unit tests, since CI already authenticates to Databricks to trigger the job.

End-to-end testing

Integration tests prove that the pipeline works. End-to-end tests prove that the system works, including the consumers downstream.

The model is served behind an endpoint, and a frontend team, a mobile app, or another service consumes it. The contract between the model and its consumer is a real interface that consists of the request format, response schema, latency expectations, error handling, and fallback behavior. It breaks in production like any other interface. End-to-end tests validate it from the consumer’s perspective.

The common failure mode looks like this:

  1. The ML team tests the pipeline, evaluates the model, and tests the endpoint in isolation.

  2. An incident still happens because the frontend expected one field and the endpoint returned another, or latency doubled after a model update, or the consumer cannot handle a class label the retrained model now outputs.

None of this is specific to ML. It is the contract testing that any service architecture needs. However, ML teams skip it disproportionately because the boundary between the model team and the product team is broader than usual, and “It’s done” gets defined as “The model is served.”

These tests run in an acceptance environment where a real model is served and either a real consumer or a realistic test harness for it calls the endpoint. These tests are slow and require coordination across teams, so they sit at the top of the pyramid: you need a few of them, but you cannot skip them.

End-to-end tests and production monitoring are two points on a continuum, rather than separate boxes. An end-to-end test validates the consumer contract at a point in time in a controlled environment. Monitoring validates the same contract continuously against real traffic. For ML systems, with their delayed labels and gradually shifting prediction distributions, some of the most important validation can only happen in production. A/B testing, which we briefly covered earlier, is one form of validation that runs against live traffic. Monitoring is the subject of the next chapter.

Conclusion

This chapter moved from model development to a structured deployment strategy built on CI/CD and DABs. The Databricks platform design provides the foundation for reliable and secure ML operations across environments, from development to acceptance to production.

We defined end-to-end ML pipelines declaratively in databricks.yml. Configuring jobs as code and passing parameters to Python tasks gives us traceability, portability, and automation, which are the key enablers of MLOps. The same bundle definition runs in every environment.

We also covered testing for ML systems, from unit tests on individual transformations, through integration tests that prove the pipeline runs, to the end-to-end tests that validate the consumer contract. The pyramid tells you how to expend effort, conducting many fast tests at the bottom and a few slow ones at the top, but skipping none of them.

In the next chapter, we’ll shift our focus to monitoring, which is the final piece that closes the loop by ensuring models stay reliable once deployed.
